title: You Can't Really Tickle Yourself #science #brain
description:
You can't really tickle yourself. When you move, your brain predicts the touch before it lands, and turns that predicted touch down, so the tickle fades. In one experiment people moved one hand while a robot stroked their other palm with soft foam; adding a delay of a fifth of a second (200 ms) made it feel more tickly.

More ways your brain edits what you sense: Why do wheels spin backwards on camera? https://youtu.be/SxjS9sdc_Ek

Sources
- Weiskrantz, L., Elliott, J. & Darlington, C. (1971), Preliminary observations on tickling oneself, Nature 230: 598–599
- Blakemore, S.-J., Wolpert, D. M. & Frith, C. D. (1998), Central cancellation of self-produced tickle sensation, Nature Neuroscience 1: 635–640
- Blakemore, S.-J., Frith, C. D. & Wolpert, D. M. (1999), Spatio-temporal prediction modulates the perception of self-produced stimuli, Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience 11(5)
- Blakemore, S.-J., Wolpert, D. & Frith, C. (2000), Why can't you tickle yourself? NeuroReport 11: R11–R16
- The tickle meter is an illustration of 'less' and 'more', not the study's rating scale

Try it: can you tickle yourself at all?
